claims.text: Machine-learned molecular-dynamics potentials can capture atomic-scale disorder, mass fluctuations, and defect-induced force-constant variations in HfNbTaTiZr.
Combining the molecular-dynamics calculation with an independent electron-scattering model can predict lattice thermal conductivity without conflating lattice and electronic transport.
The proposed approach will predict lattice-only thermal conductivity of nominally oxygen-free HfNbTaTiZr within ±10% of experimental values between 100 and 200 K.
Between 300 and 1200 K, intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity of oxygen-free HfNbTaTiZr will be significantly greater than 10–17 W/(K·m).
An oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr specimen has a measured total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Nominally oxygen-free HfNbTaTiZr contains inherent atomic-mass variations, force-constant diversity, and natural defect structures.
The machine-learned potentials will be calibrated using DFT-derived phonon and elastic data on large statistical supercells.
The separate electron-scattering model will be parameterized using low-temperature electron-mobility data.
The simulations will cover 100–1200 K using large disordered supercells with realistic atomic-scale variations.
Mass fluctuations, defects, and force-constant distributions provide local structural variations that mediate thermal transport.
Molecular dynamics resolves anharmonic phonon interactions and defect-induced phonon scattering.
Resolving anharmonic and defect-induced scattering enables an independent calculation of lattice heat transport.
A separate electron-scattering calculation can quantify the electronic contribution and permit decoupled analysis of lattice and electronic transport.
Existing models based on perfect, defect-free crystals tend to conflate lattice and electronic contributions or misestimate absolute conductivity.
The prediction is applicable only to nominally oxygen-free HfNbTaTiZr over 100–1200 K.
The approach may be unreliable below 100 K because quantum effects dominate.
The approach may be unreliable for samples with significant oxygen contamination.
Deviation by more than ±10% from lattice-only measurements below 200 K would falsify the low-temperature prediction.
Failure of the separated high-temperature transport predictions to align with independent measurements would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The applicability boundary excludes temperatures below 100 K, but the experiment and falsification rule refer broadly to measurements 'below 200 K' without imposing the 100 K lower limit, potentially treating out-of-domain data as decisive.
